notes: Trudeau majority government, no coalition: slot 1 holds the PC opposition. Waffle in 5 (New Left), FLQ in 19 (national-liberation Marxism), PQ in 18 following MD's BQ placement, Ralliement créditiste in 20, Union Nationale (governing Quebec) in 14, western Social Credit in 16. No MD sprites available for CAN, so all icons null.

0.name: RCMP Security Service
0.text:
The Security Service is the counter-intelligence and counter-subversion arm of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, answering to Commissioner William Higgitt. Ottawa has just accepted the Mackenzie Commission's call to give it a more civilian character, but it remains a police directorate watching Soviet-bloc diplomats, communists, Quebec separatists and campus radicals.

Its outlook is that of the Cold War front line: close liaison with the FBI, the CIA and MI5, files on thousands of Canadians, and wiretaps in Montreal. It has no voters, but in a domestic emergency it would have the government's ear and the War Measures Act at its back.

1.name: Progressive Conservative Party of Canada
1.text:
The Progressive Conservative Party is Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, holding 72 seats after its defeat in the June 1968 election. Its leader is Robert Stanfield, the former Premier of Nova Scotia, chosen in 1967 to succeed John Diefenbaker, who still sits in the caucus and resents the new course.

The Tories stand for fiscal prudence, the Crown and loyalty to NATO and the Commonwealth, while Stanfield courts Quebec with a conciliatory tone that the Diefenbaker wing rejects. Their strength lies in the Prairies, rural Ontario and the Atlantic provinces, and among voters wary of Trudeau's centralism.

2.name: Liberal Party of Canada
2.text:
The Liberal Party of Canada governs with the majority it won in June 1968 on a wave of 'Trudeaumania'. Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau, a Montreal law professor who entered Parliament only in 1965, leads a cabinet that includes John Turner, Mitchell Sharp and Jean Marchand.

Trudeau's 'Just Society' promises official bilingualism, a reformed Criminal Code and a strong federal state able to defeat Quebec separatism. Abroad he is reviewing Canada's role in NATO, has cut the forces in Europe and is negotiating recognition of the People's Republic of China. The party dominates Quebec and the big cities and sees itself as the natural governing party.

3.name: New Democratic Party
3.text:
The New Democratic Party, founded in 1961 by the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation and the Canadian Labour Congress, holds 22 seats in the Commons. It is led by Tommy Douglas, the former Premier of Saskatchewan who built medicare, while Ed Schreyer has just made Manitoba an NDP province.

The party champions public health insurance, stronger labour rights, progressive taxation and Canadian control of the economy, and it is wary of NATO and the Vietnam War. Its base is organised labour, Prairie farmers and urban intellectuals; its leverage lies in minority Parliaments and provincial power, though the radical Waffle now challenges its leadership from within.

4.name: Communist Party of Canada
4.text:
The Communist Party of Canada, founded in 1921, is a legal but marginal party loyal to Moscow. General Secretary William Kashtan has led it since 1965, while the veteran Tim Buck remains its honoured national chairman. It holds no seats and won only a few thousand votes in 1968.

The party calls for withdrawal from NATO and NORAD, an independent foreign policy, nationalisation of key industries and Canadian ownership of resources. Its influence lies in a handful of unions, the Canadian Tribune, ethnic organisations among Ukrainian and Finnish Canadians and the peace movement, while the RCMP watches its every move.

5.name: The Waffle
5.text:
The Waffle is the New Left caucus inside the NDP, born in 1969 around the manifesto 'For an Independent Socialist Canada'. Its leading figures are the economist Mel Watkins, author of the 1968 federal report on foreign ownership, and the young historian James Laxer, backed by students and younger unionists.

It argues that Canada is becoming an American branch-plant economy and that only public ownership can win back independence. It opposes the Vietnam War, NATO and NORAD, and accepts Quebec's right to self-determination. At the 1969 Winnipeg convention its manifesto won over a third of the delegates, enough to frighten the party establishment.

6.name: Canadian Peace Congress
6.text:
The Canadian Peace Congress is the national section of the Soviet-sponsored World Peace Council, founded in 1949. It is led by Dr James Endicott, the former missionary in China and Stalin Peace Prize laureate, and draws on communist and fellow-travelling activists.

Its programme follows the Moscow line on disarmament: withdrawal from NATO and NORAD, an end to American nuclear weapons on Canadian soil and solidarity with North Vietnam. It condemns Washington while staying silent on Prague. Its leverage is modest, resting on a few churches, ethnic halls and the anti-war mood among students.

7.name: Association of United Ukrainian Canadians
7.text:
The Association of United Ukrainian Canadians is the pro-Soviet wing of Ukrainian Canada, heir to the Ukrainian Labour Farmer Temple Association banned in 1940. It runs labour temples, choirs, dance ensembles and the newspaper Zhyttia i Slovo, and is closely tied to the Communist Party.

It praises Soviet Ukraine, sends delegations to Kiev and attacks the nationalist émigré organisations that dominate the community. Its membership is ageing and shrinking, but it provides money, halls and disciplined cadres in Winnipeg, Toronto and Edmonton, and it is a channel for Soviet cultural diplomacy that the RCMP watches closely.

8.name: Al-Majlis al-Ja'fari
8.text:
Al-Majlis al-Ja'fari is a small circle of Lebanese Shia families and students in Montreal and Ottawa who gather for Muharram majalis in rented halls and private homes. Many come from Jabal Amil and follow the reforming cleric Musa al-Sadr, who has just been elected to lead the new Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut.

It seeks religious instruction for Canadian-born children, a first Shia prayer hall and recognition alongside the Sunni-led mosques. Its outlook is moderate and communal: loyal to Canada, sympathetic to Arab causes and wary of politics. Its weight lies in family networks and links to merchants in Beirut and West Africa.

9.name: Shabab al-Najaf
9.text:
Shabab al-Najaf is a tiny network of Iraqi, Iranian and Lebanese Shia students at McGill, the Université de Montréal and Toronto who pass around the sermons of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf since 1965. They meet quietly, aware that the Shah's agents watch Iranian students abroad.

They reject the Shah, the Ba'athist regime in Baghdad and Western influence alike, and argue that a just Islamic government must be led by the jurists. Their numbers are negligible, but they are disciplined, fluent in Persian and Arabic polemic, and connected to similar circles in Europe and the United States.

10.name: Rabitat al-'Alam al-Islami
10.text:
The Muslim World League, founded in Mecca in 1962 with Saudi backing, reaches into Canada through scholarships, Qur'ans and literature sent to the country's few mosques. Its influence is felt in Edmonton's Al Rashid Mosque and in Montreal and Toronto, where Arab and South Asian congregations depend on outside funds.

It promotes a conservative, establishment Sunni Islam loyal to King Faisal, hostile to communism and to Nasser's secular nationalism. Politically quietist inside Canada, it presents itself as a partner of Western governments against atheism, and its leverage lies in money, imams trained in Arabia and the prestige of the Holy Places.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, has a few sympathisers among Arab students in Montreal and Toronto. They pass on the party's pamphlets from Beirut and Amman and recruit through informal study circles.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and both Cold War blocs, calling for a single caliphate to unite all Muslims under Islamic law. It forbids armed struggle by its members but seeks the support of army officers in Muslim lands. In Canada it is insignificant in numbers, but its message appeals to students embittered by the 1967 defeat.

12.name: Muslim Students' Association
12.text:
The Muslim Students' Association of the United States and Canada, founded in 1963 at the University of Illinois, has chapters at McGill, Toronto, Windsor and other campuses. Its organisers are largely Arab and South Asian graduate students, many shaped by the Muslim Brotherhood and Jamaat-e-Islami.

The association runs Friday prayers, summer conferences and translations of Hasan al-Banna, Sayyid Qutb and Mawdudi, building an Islamic identity among students far from home. It is cautious in Canadian politics, critical of Israel and of secular Arab regimes, and its leverage lies in a growing continental network and the professionals it trains.

13.name: Privy Council Office
13.text:
The Privy Council Office is the central secretariat of the federal government, led by Clerk Gordon Robertson. Under Trudeau it has grown into a powerful machine of planners and policy advisers, with the young Michael Pitfield among its rising mandarins.

Its outlook is rational planning above party: cabinet committees, systems analysis and a strong federal state able to manage the economy and contain Quebec nationalism. Together with the Prime Minister's Office under Marc Lalonde, it decides what reaches cabinet, and in any crisis it would draft the measures and run the machinery of state.

14.name: Union nationale
14.text:
The Union Nationale governs Quebec under Premier Jean-Jacques Bertrand, who succeeded Daniel Johnson after his death in 1968. Founded in 1935 by Maurice Duplessis, it rules from the countryside, but faces an election this year with a divided caucus and a reviving Liberal opposition.

It is a conservative nationalist party defending provincial autonomy, Catholic tradition and rural Quebec, and it demands far more powers from Ottawa. Its controversial Bill 63 on language rights has alienated nationalists, but it still holds patronage networks in every parish and county of the province.

15.name: Argus Corporation
15.text:
Argus Corporation is the Toronto holding company that controls Massey-Ferguson, Dominion Stores, Domtar, Hollinger Mines and Standard Broadcasting. Founded in 1945 by E. P. Taylor, it is now steered by John A. 'Bud' McDougald, the epitome of the Bay Street establishment.

Argus and its allies on the boards of the big chartered banks favour low taxes, free capital flows and close integration with the American market, and they view Trudeau's planners with suspicion. Their leverage lies in boardrooms, Toronto clubs and political donations, which flow to both old parties.

16.name: Social Credit Party of Canada
16.text:
The Social Credit Party of Canada lost all its seats in 1968, yet Social Credit still governs British Columbia under W. A. C. Bennett and Alberta under Harry Strom. The federal party survives as a shell, separate from the Quebec Créditistes.

In the West it has become a free-enterprise, anti-socialist coalition: low taxes, provincial development of dams and highways, and hostility to Ottawa's spending and to the NDP. Its monetary-reform roots are now mostly rhetoric. Its leverage is provincial power, evangelical Protestant voters and business backers who see it as the bulwark against socialism.

17.name: Pollution Probe
17.text:
Pollution Probe was founded in February 1969 by students and professors at the University of Toronto. Its young organisers, advised by the zoologist Donald Chant, have already staged a mock funeral for the polluted Don River and are pressing Queen's Park on DDT and smog.

It calls for strict pollution laws, bans on dangerous pesticides and phosphate detergents, and public accountability for industry. It speaks for a new environmental consciousness among students and suburban families, and its leverage lies in media campaigns, scientific credibility and alliances with conservationists across the country.

18.name: Parti Québécois
18.text:
The Parti Québécois was founded in October 1968 by René Lévesque, the former Liberal minister, who merged his Mouvement souveraineté-association with the Ralliement national. Members of the dissolved Rassemblement pour l'indépendance nationale have joined, and the party prepares for its first Quebec election.

It proposes sovereignty for Quebec in an economic association with Canada, French as the language of work and a social-democratic state that would take control of key resources. Its support lies among students, teachers, unionists and the francophone middle class, and its leverage grows with every quarrel over language and the constitution.

19.name: Front de libération du Québec
19.text:
The Front de libération du Québec is an underground network of autonomous cells that has carried out bombings in Montreal since 1963, including the attack on the Montreal Stock Exchange in February 1969. Its theorists Pierre Vallières and Charles Gagnon are in prison awaiting trial.

It preaches an independent, socialist Quebec won through armed struggle, inspired by Cuba, Algeria and the anti-colonial movements, and denounces Anglo-American imperialism. It has no fixed leadership, only scattered cells of young militants, but its capacity for terror and its sympathy among radicalised youth make it the gravest threat to public order in Canada.

20.name: Ralliement créditiste
20.text:
The Ralliement créditiste is the Quebec Social Credit party of Réal Caouette, a car dealer and fiery television orator from Rouyn-Noranda. It broke with the English-Canadian Social Credit Party in 1963 and won 14 seats in rural Quebec in 1968.

It rails against bankers, high interest, big government and the 'dictatorship of finance', defends Catholic morality, the small farmer and the merchant, and attacks both Trudeau's elites and the separatists. Its strength lies in Abitibi, the Beauce and other poor rural ridings, where Caouette's populism outshines the established parties.

21.name: Edmund Burke Society
21.text:
The Edmund Burke Society was founded in Toronto in 1967 by Paul Fromm, Don Andrews and Leigh Smith as a militant anti-communist group. It pickets peace marches, brawls with leftist students and is drifting toward open white nationalism.

It preaches the defence of Western Christian civilisation against communism, immigration from the Third World and liberal permissiveness, and admires Rhodesia and South Africa. Its numbers are small, but it is the most active cell of the far right in Canada, linked to older antisemitic circles around John Ross Taylor.

22.name: Canadian Armed Forces
22.text:
The Canadian Armed Forces were unified in February 1968, merging the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force into a single service. General Frederick Sharp is Chief of the Defence Staff, presiding over a force of under 100,000 facing budget cuts.

The officer corps is loyal to Parliament and to NATO, and resents Trudeau's decision to halve the brigade in Germany and the loss of the old regimental and naval identities. It has no political tradition, but in a domestic crisis the government can call it out in aid of the civil power.

23.name: House of Windsor
23.text:
Elizabeth II is Queen of Canada, represented in Ottawa by Governor General Roland Michener, a former Speaker of the House of Commons. The Crown is the formal head of the federal and provincial governments and the focus of the loyalist traditions of Ontario and the Maritimes.

Monarchists defend the Crown as a symbol of continuity, of parliamentary government and of Canada's distinctness from the United States, and they resist republican and separatist sentiment in Quebec. Their leverage lies in the armed forces, veterans' associations, the Orange Order and English-Canadian sentiment, though the Crown itself stays above politics.
